ANSWER — 29 C.F.R. § 825.200(a) (general FMLA entitlement, military caregiver leave set aside)

1) AMOUNT: 12 workweeks.
2) PERIOD: any 12-month period (the 12-month period the employer has selected under § 825.200(b)).
3) The 26-workweek entitlement to care for a covered servicemember with a serious injury or illness (§ 825.200(f)–(g); § 825.127) is excluded from both answers above and is discussed below only to set it aside.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
I. CONTROLLING TEXT (verbatim, § 825.200(a))
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
"§ 825.200 Amount of leave.
(a) Except in the case of leave to care for a covered servicemember with a serious injury or illness, an eligible employee's FMLA leave entitlement is limited to a total of 12 workweeks of leave during any 12-month period for any one, or more, of the following reasons:
(1) The birth of the employee's son or daughter, and to care for the newborn child;
(2) The placement with the employee of a son or daughter for adoption or foster care, and to care for the newly placed child;
(3) To care for the employee's spouse, son, daughter, or parent with a serious health condition;
(4) Because of a serious health condition that makes the employee unable to perform one or more of the essential functions of his or her job; and,
(5) Because of any qualifying exigency arising out of the fact that the employee's spouse, son, daughter, or parent is a military member on covered active duty status (or has been notified of an impending call or order to covered active duty)."

Every operative word of the answer is in that sentence: "limited to a total of 12 workweeks of leave during any 12-month period."

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
II. HOW EACH ASK IS ANSWERED FROM THE TEXT
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Ask 1 — Amount: "12 workweeks." The figure is a ceiling ("limited to a total of"), not a floor the employee may be given less than; an employer may be more generous by policy, CBA, or state law, but the federal FMLA entitlement is capped at 12 workweeks.
  • It is 12 workweeks in the aggregate, not 12 per reason. The phrase "for any one, or more, of the following reasons" means an employee who takes 6 weeks for birth/bonding and 6 weeks for the employee's own serious health condition has used the full 12-week entitlement for that 12-month period.
  • It is not scaled to hours worked. A part-time employee is still entitled to 12 workweeks; the entitlement is applied by converting workweeks into hours — 12 × the number of hours the employee normally works per week (e.g., a 20-hour/week employee has 240 hours of FMLA leave available in the 12-month period). Deduction rules for intermittent leave and reduced schedules are in § 825.205 (outside paragraph (a)).

Ask 2 — Period: "any 12-month period." Section 825.200(a) fixes the length of the measuring period (12 months) but not its start date. The employer selects the method, per § 825.200(b):
  "(1) The calendar year;
   (2) Any fixed 12-month leave year, such as a fiscal year, a year required by State law, or a year starting on an employee's anniversary date;
   (3) The 12-month period measured forward from the date any employee's first FMLA leave under paragraph (a) begins; or,
   (4) A 'rolling' 12-month period measured backward from the date an employee uses any FMLA leave as described in paragraph (a)."
  Therefore the correct statement of the period is "any 12-month period, as determined by the employer's selected method under § 825.200(b)" — not a calendar year and not a rolling period as a matter of law. The remainder of § 825.200 requires the chosen method to be applied consistently and uniformly to all employees and supplies a default (the method most beneficial to the employee) where the employer has not selected one; those mechanics are outside paragraph (a) and do not change the 12-month length.

Ask 3 — The servicemember carve-out, set aside: paragraph (a) opens with "Except in the case of leave to care for a covered servicemember with a serious injury or illness." That clause removes military caregiver leave from the 12-workweek computation. The excluded entitlement is:
  "(f) An eligible employee's FMLA leave entitlement is limited to a total of 26 workweeks of leave during a single 12-month period to care for a covered servicemember with a serious injury or illness. An employer shall determine the single 12-month period in which the 26-weeks-of-leave-entitlement described in this paragraph occurs using the 12-month period measured forward from the date an employee's first FMLA leave to care for the covered servicemember begins. See § 825.127(e)(1).
   (g) During the single 12-month period described in paragraph (f), an eligible employee's FMLA leave entitlement is limited to a combined total of 26 workweeks of FMLA leave for any qualifying reason. See § 825.127(e)(3)."
  Operation of the carve-out, for completeness only: the 26 weeks runs in its own "single 12-month period" measured forward from the first day of military caregiver leave, regardless of the employer's (b) method; within that period the employee may still take up to 12 weeks for reasons (1)–(5), with a combined ceiling of 26 weeks (e.g., 12 weeks bonding + 14 weeks military caregiver = 26, permissible; 16 weeks bonding + 10 weeks military caregiver = not permissible). None of this modifies the 12 workweeks / any 12-month period answer above.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
III. SCOPE LIMITS ON THESE TWO NUMBERS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
• Eligibility is a separate question. "Eligible employee" is defined by § 825.110 (12 months of employment and 1,250 hours of service in the 12 months preceding leave, plus the 50-employee/75-mile tests on the employer side). Those conditions gate whether the 12 workweeks is owed at all; they do not alter its size.
• One express statutory/regulatory variant on the measure: eligible airline flight crew employees receive 72 days (12 workweeks × a uniform 6-day workweek) under § 825.802(a)(1), and 156 days of military caregiver leave under § 825.802(a)(2). That is a special calculation rule for a defined class, not a different reading of § 825.200(a); for all other employees the measure is 12 workweeks.
• The FMLA entitlement is a floor of federal protection only. More generous leave under an employer policy, a collective bargaining agreement, or state/local law may exist and is unaffected; § 825.200(a) caps the FMLA entitlement, it does not cap those other sources.
• Unused FMLA leave need not carry over; § 825.200(a) grants 12 workweeks within each 12-month period rather than a bank that accumulates across periods.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
IV. ONE-LINE HOLDING
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Leaving aside leave to care for a covered servicemember with a serious injury or illness, an eligible employee's FMLA entitlement under 29 C.F.R. § 825.200(a) is a total of 12 workweeks of leave during any 12-month period — the 12-month period being whichever 12-month method the employer has adopted under § 825.200(b) — for any one or more of the five qualifying reasons listed in (a)(1)–(5).

The first reads: "This entitlement is based on a uniform six-day workweek for all airline flight crew employees, regardless of time actually worked or paid, multiplied by the statutory 26-workweek entitlement for military caregiver leave."

RFC 5321 §4.5.3.1 — MAXIMUM LINE LENGTHS FOR SMTP TEXT LINE AND REPLY LINE, AND WHAT THE COUNTS INCLUDE

=========================================================================
1. ANSWER AT A GLANCE
=========================================================================

  Line type      | Max total length | Counted in the total                                  | Section
  ---------------|------------------|-------------------------------------------------------|---------
  Command line   | 512 octets       | command word + all arguments/parameters + <CRLF>      | 4.5.3.1.4
  Reply line     | 512 octets       | reply code + [SP + reply text] + <CRLF>               | 4.5.3.1.5
  Text line      | 1000 octets      | the line's content + <CRLF>; the leading dot         | 4.5.3.1.6
                 |                  | duplicated for transparency is NOT counted            |

  Direct answer to the question as worded:
    * SMTP TEXT LINE  -> 1000 octets maximum total length (§4.5.3.1.6).
    * SMTP REPLY LINE -> 512 octets maximum total length (§4.5.3.1.5).

  Terminology warning, stated up front because it is the usual source of
error: RFC 5321 gives 'Text Line' its own definition (§4.5.3.1.6) and it is
NOT the command line. The command line limit is 512 octets (§4.5.3.1.4).
If the question meant the command line rather than the defined term 'Text
Line', the figure is 512 octets, not 1000. Both figures are given above so
the answer is correct under either reading, but the 1000-octet number
belongs only to Text Line (i.e., message content lines sent in DATA).

=========================================================================
2. VERBATIM SOURCE TEXT (RFC 5321, October 2008, §4.5.3.1)
=========================================================================

§4.5.3.1.4.  Command Line
  "The maximum total length of a command line including the command word
   and the <CRLF> is 512 octets.  SMTP extensions may be used to increase
   this limit."

§4.5.3.1.5.  Reply Line
  "The maximum total length of a reply line including the reply code and
   the <CRLF> is 512 octets.  More information may be conveyed through
   multiple-line replies."

§4.5.3.1.6.  Text Line
  "The maximum total length of a text line including the <CRLF> is 1000
   octets (not counting the leading dot duplicated for transparency).
   This number may be increased by the use of SMTP Service Extensions."

Preamble of §4.5.3.1 (the clause preserved in the fetched excerpt):
  "... in octets where absolute lengths, rather than character counts,
   are intended."

Source: RFC 5321, J. Klensin, October 2008 —
https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc5321/ (fetched 2026-11-17T05:21:31Z,
sha256 5e893bb90b68), corroborated by
https://www.hjp.at/(en,st_a)/doc/rfc/rfc5321.html (sha256 ed3e6520c7d1).
(Read the opening paragraph of §4.5.3.1 in the RFC itself for the full
minimum/maximum framing sentence; only the clause above is quoted here
because only that clause is present in the retrieved text.)

=========================================================================
3. WHAT THE COUNTS INCLUDE (the second part of the question)
=========================================================================

Four rules govern all three figures:

(a) The counts are OCTETS, not characters.  §4.5.3.1 measures "in octets
    where absolute lengths, rather than character counts, are intended."
    An octet is 8 bits.  For pure US-ASCII these coincide, but the limit is
defined on octets, so any 8-bit or non-ASCII material (e.g., under an
extension) is counted by bytes on the wire, not by code points.

(b) The terminating <CRLF> IS included.  <CRLF> is two octets: CR = %d13
    (0x0D) and LF = %d10 (0x0A).  Every one of the 512 / 512 / 1000 figures
is a total-length figure that already contains those two octets.

(c) Specifically, per line type:
      COMMAND LINE — includes the command verb (e.g., "MAIL", "RCPT",
        "EHLO"), every space, every parameter and argument (reverse-path,
forward-path, EHLO domain, ESMTP parameters such as SIZE=...), and the
trailing <CRLF>.  Nothing in the command is excluded.
      REPLY LINE — includes the three-digit reply code, the separator that
        follows it (SP for the final line, "-" for a continuation line of
        a multiline reply), the reply text (including any enhanced status
        code such as 2.1.0, which is ordinary reply text), and the trailing
        <CRLF>.  Note §4.4.2's rule that the space following the reply code
is considered part of the text, and that the SP may be omitted (servers
SHOULD send it; clients MUST accept its absence).
      TEXT LINE — includes the entire content of the line plus the trailing
        <CRLF>, with one explicit exclusion: the leading dot that is
        duplicated for transparency (dot-stuffing, §4.5.2) is not counted.
        The original single leading dot, if present, is part of the content
and therefore is counted; only the *duplicate* added for transparency is
free.

(d) These are single-line limits, and extensions may raise them.
      §4.5.3.1.4 says SMTP extensions may increase the command-line limit;
      §4.5.3.1.6 says the text-line number may be increased by SMTP Service
      Extensions; §4.5.3.1.5 offers no extension escape hatch but points to
      multiple-line replies as the way to carry more information.

=========================================================================
4. DERIVED WORKING NUMBERS (payload budgets, CRLF removed)
=========================================================================

  Command line : 512 total − 2 (CRLF) = 510 octets of command text max.
                 e.g. "MAIL FROM:<user@example.com> SIZE=1000000\r\n"
                 = 41 + 2 = 43 octets (well inside 512).

  Reply line   : 512 total − 2 (CRLF) = 510 octets after removing CRLF.
                 Minus 3 (reply code) minus 1 (SP or "-") = 506 octets of
                 reply text max in the normal "NNN<SP>text" / "NNN-text"
                 form.  If the SP is omitted, the text field may be 507
                 octets (510 − 3).  Either way the whole line stays ≤ 512.
                 e.g. "250 2.1.0 Sender OK\r\n" = 19 + 2 = 21 octets.
                 Enhanced status codes are not granted extra room by
                 §4.5.3.1; they are spent out of the same 506-octet budget.

  Text line    : 1000 total − 2 (CRLF) = 998 octets of content max.
                 Transparency: if the content begins with '.', the wire
                 carries one extra '.' that §4.5.3.1.6 excludes from the
                 count.  Worst-case wire length is therefore
                 998 + 1 (duplicated dot) + 2 (CRLF) = 1001 octets, and that
                 line is still compliant.  The 1001 figure is an
                 on-the-wire size, not a breach of the 1000-octet limit.

  Multiline reply: each constituent line is independently subject to the
                 512-octet reply-line limit; k lines can carry up to
                 k × 506 octets of text.  §4.5.3.1.5 sets no aggregate cap
                 on the reply as a whole.

=========================================================================
5. POINTS THAT ARE COMMONLY GOT WRONG
=========================================================================

  1. 512 vs 1000.  Applying the 1000-octet Text Line limit to commands (or
     to replies) is wrong; 1000 applies only to message content lines in
     DATA.  Conversely, 512 is not a limit on DATA content lines.
  2. CRLF counted as one.  Older documents and some implementations count
     CRLF as a single line terminator; RFC 5321 counts it as two octets
     inside the 512/512/1000 totals.
  3. Character vs octet.  The limits are octets; a length computed in
     characters is not equivalent once non-ASCII octets are on the wire.
  4. Dot-stuffing.  The duplicated dot is free, but the original dot is
     not; and the CRLF is never free.
  5. Multiline replies.  The 512-octet cap is per line, not per reply.
  6. Unverified claim to reject: a "64-octet allowance for enhanced status
     codes" inside §4.5.3.1.  No such sentence appears in the retrieved
     §4.5.3.1 text.  If a specification or code comment cites one, it must
     be traced to its actual source before being relied on; §4.5.3.1 as
     quoted above grants no such carve-out, and enhanced status codes are
     simply part of the 506-octet reply-text budget.

=========================================================================
6. PRACTICAL APPLICATION (how to size buffers against these limits)
=========================================================================

  * Read a command line with a cap of 512 octets including CRLF; a buffer
    of 513 octets plus an explicit overlong-line check is sufficient
    (anything requiring more than 512 octets before CRLF is a 500-class
    error / line-too-long condition).
  * Read a reply line with a cap of 512 octets including CRLF; continue
    reading additional lines while the 4th octet is '-' (multiline reply).
  * Read a DATA line with a cap of 1000 octets including CRLF, counting the
    line as received *before* removing the transparency dot; i.e., accept
    up to 1001 octets on the wire when the line begins with '.', and strip
    the duplicate dot before length-checking the content against 998.

=========================================================================
7. CITATIONS FOR VERIFICATION
=========================================================================

  RFC 5321, October 2008, §4.5.3.1.4 (Command Line), §4.5.3.1.5 (Reply
  Line), §4.5.3.1.6 (Text Line); related: §4.4.2 (multiline reply format,
  SP after reply code treated as part of the text), §4.5.2 (transparency /
  dot-stuffing).  Primary text: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc5321/
  (fetched 2026-11-17T05:21:31Z, sha256 5e893bb90b68); mirror:
  https://www.hjp.at/(en,st_a)/doc/rfc/rfc5321.html (sha256 ed3e6520c7d1).

## 49 CFR 395.3(a) — property-carrying CMV: the three limits

### Source and currency
Current text of 49 CFR 395.3 (eCFR, Title 49, Subtitle B, Chapter III, Subchapter B, Part 395, Subpart A), fetched 2026-11-17. Source credit line on the section: "[76 FR 81188, Dec. 27, 2011, as amended at 78 FR 58485, Sept. 24, 2013; 78 FR 64181, Oct. 28, 2013; 84 FR 48081, Sept. 12, 2019; 85 FR 33452, June 1, 2020]" — i.e., the 2020 amendments are the latest, so the 10/14/11 figures below are the current-vintage figures.

### The answers

| Ask | Answer | Citation |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Consecutive hours off duty required before driving | **10 consecutive hours off duty** | § 395.3(a)(1) |
| 2. Consecutive hours after which the driver may no longer drive | **14 consecutive hours** (measured from coming on duty, following 10 consecutive hours off duty) | § 395.3(a)(2) |
| 3. Total hours that may be driven within that period | **11 hours** of driving within the 14-hour period | § 395.3(a)(3)(i) |

### Governing text (verbatim)

**§ 395.3(a) preamble:** "Except as otherwise provided in § 395.1, no motor carrier shall permit or require any driver used by it to drive a property-carrying commercial motor vehicle, nor shall any such driver drive a property-carrying commercial motor vehicle, regardless of the number of motor carriers using the driver's services, unless the driver complies with the following requirements:"

**(a)(1) Start of work shift.** "A driver may not drive without first taking 10 consecutive hours off duty;"

**(a)(2) 14-hour period.** "A driver may not drive after a period of 14 consecutive hours after coming on-duty following 10 consecutive hours off-duty."

**(a)(3)(i) Driving time.** "A driver may drive a total of 11 hours during the period specified in paragraph (a)(2) of this section."

**(a)(3)(ii) Interruption of driving time.** "Except for drivers who qualify for either of the short-haul exceptions in § 395.1(e)(1) or (2), driving is not permitted if more than 8 hours of driving time have passed without at least a consecutive 30-minute interruption in driving status. A consecutive 30-minute interruption of driving status may be satisfied either by off-duty, sleeper berth or on-duty not driving time or by a combination of off-duty, sleeper berth and on-duty not driving time."

### Plain-language restatement

1. **Reset (10 hours).** The driver cannot drive at all until 10 consecutive hours off duty have been taken. This is a continuous block; it is the qualifying event that starts the next work shift.
2. **Duty window (14 hours).** Once the driver comes on duty after that 10-hour block, a 14-consecutive-hour clock starts. When 14 hours have elapsed, driving must stop — even if the driver has not yet used all 11 driving hours. The driver may still perform on-duty-not-driving work after hour 14; the prohibition is on driving.
3. **Driving cap (11 hours).** Within those 14 hours, no more than 11 hours may be spent in driving status. A driver who reaches 11 hours of driving must stop driving even if the 14-hour window has time left.

Whichever ceiling is reached first — 11 hours of driving or 14 elapsed hours — ends driving for that shift.

### Interpretation points that matter for correct application

- **The 14 hours is elapsed time, not accumulated on-duty time.** The question is phrased as "consecutive hours on duty," but (a)(2) measures 14 consecutive hours *after coming on duty*. Off-duty or sleeper-berth time taken inside the shift does not pause or extend that clock (subject only to the split-sleeper-berth provision at § 395.1(g), which is an exception to (a), not part of it). This is the single most common misapplication of the rule.
- **The 11 hours is driving time, not on-duty time.** On-duty-not-driving time (loading, fueling, paperwork, inspections) consumes the 14-hour window but not the 11-hour driving allowance.
- **A 30-minute interruption is a separate, additional requirement.** Under (a)(3)(ii), a driver may not drive after more than 8 cumulative hours of driving without at least a consecutive 30-minute interruption in driving status (satisfiable by off-duty, sleeper berth, on-duty-not-driving, or any combination). This does not extend the 14-hour window and does not increase the 11-hour cap; it can force a stop before either limit is reached.
- **The three limits are independent and all binding.** Compliance requires satisfying all of them simultaneously; the binding constraint on any given day is whichever is hit first.

### Limits outside § 395.3(a) that can bind earlier

These do not change the three answers, but a reader should not treat the (a) figures as the only ceilings:

- **§ 395.3(b) — cycle limits.** No driving after 60 hours on duty in any 7 consecutive days (carrier not operating every day of the week) or 70 hours on duty in any 8 consecutive days (carrier operating every day). A driver can be legal on the 10/14/11 rule and still be out of hours on the cycle rule.
- **§ 395.3(c) — 34-hour restart.** Any 7- or 8-consecutive-day period may end with the beginning of an off-duty period of 34 or more consecutive hours, which resets the (b) cycle calculation.
- **§ 395.1(b)(1) — adverse driving conditions.** Up to 2 additional hours beyond the § 395.3(a) maximums to complete the run or reach a place of safety, when adverse conditions as defined in § 395.2 prevent safe completion within the normal limits. This extends the driving/duty maximums; it is an exception to (a), and the (a) rule itself opens with "Except as otherwise provided in § 395.1."
- **§ 395.1(e) — short-haul (150 air-mile radius).** Drivers meeting the § 395.1(e)(1) conditions are exempt from the § 395.8 records-of-duty-status requirement and are excepted from the (a)(3)(ii) 30-minute interruption rule; the 10-consecutive-hours-off-duty / 14-consecutive-hours-on-duty structure is retained in § 395.1(e)(1)(iii)(A). The 11-hour driving cap is not the operative limit for these drivers, but the 14-hour return-and-release condition is.
- **§ 395.1(g) — split sleeper berth.** Allows the 10-hour off-duty and 14-hour window requirements to be satisfied by paired qualifying periods rather than one 10-hour block.
- **State-specific variations.** Alaska drivers of property-carrying CMVs are governed by § 395.1(h)(1) instead (15 hours following 10 consecutive hours off duty; no driving after 20 hours on duty), because § 395.3(a) and (b) do not apply there. No other state variation is assumed.

### Scope statement

The three figures above are the base rule of § 395.3(a) for a property-carrying CMV driver, stated as the regulation states them. They are not a legal opinion and do not apply the exceptions in § 395.1 (adverse conditions, short-haul, Alaska, split sleeper berth) or the cycle limits in § 395.3(b)–(c); where any of those applies, the operative limits differ and must be computed for the specific operation.

MEMORANDUM — RIGHT OF RESCISSION UNDER 12 CFR § 1026.23(a)(3)(i)

I. QUESTION PRESENTED
(1) Under § 1026.23(a)(3)(i), until when may a consumer exercise the right to rescind a covered credit transaction?
(2) When does that right expire if the required notice or the material disclosures are never delivered?

II. SHORT ANSWERS
(1) Until midnight of the third business day following the LAST of three events: (A) consummation of the transaction; (B) delivery of the notice of right to rescind required by § 1026.23(b); (C) delivery of all material disclosures. The period runs from whichever of those three occurs LAST.
(2) The right expires 3 years after consummation, upon transfer of all of the consumer's interest in the property, or upon sale of the property — WHICHEVER OCCURS FIRST. The 3-year date is a hard stop, not extended by the 3-business-day rule.

III. GOVERING TEXT (verbatim, § 1026.23(a)(3))
"(i) The consumer may exercise the right to rescind until midnight of the third business day following consummation, delivery of the notice required by paragraph (b) of this section, or delivery of all material disclosures, whichever occurs last. If the required notice or material disclosures are not delivered, the right to rescind shall expire 3 years after consummation, upon transfer of all of the consumer's interest in the property, or upon sale of the property, whichever occurs first. In the case of certain administrative proceedings, the rescission period shall be extended in accordance with section 125(f) of the Act.
(ii) For purposes of this paragraph (a)(3), the term 'material disclosures' means the required disclosures of the annual percentage rate, the finance charge, the amount financed, the total of payments, the payment schedule, and the disclosures and limitations referred to in §§ 1026.32(c) and (d) and 1026.43(g)."
Statutory source: 15 U.S.C. § 1635(a) and (f); § 1026.23 implements it for closed-end credit. (Open-end/HELOC plans are governed by the parallel § 1026.15(a)(3), which is NOT the provision asked about here.)

IV. ANALYSIS — ASK 1 (ORDINARY WINDOW)
A. Threshold coverage. The right exists "in a credit transaction in which a security interest is or will be retained or acquired in a consumer's principal dwelling," for each consumer whose ownership interest is subject to that security interest (§ 1026.23(a)(1)). Excluded under § 1026.23(f): residential mortgage transactions; refinancings/consolidations by the same creditor of debt already secured by the principal dwelling (except as to new money); transactions where a state agency is the creditor; later advances in a series where notice and all material disclosures were given; and renewals of optional insurance premiums not treated as a refinancing.
B. The three triggering events. The clock does not run from consummation alone. It runs from the latest of:
   A. consummation;
   B. delivery of the § 1026.23(b) notice (two copies to each consumer entitled to rescind, or one copy each if delivered electronically in compliance with the E-Sign Act);
   C. delivery of all material disclosures.
If the notice is delivered after consummation, the period does not begin until delivery. If the disclosures are late, the period does not begin until they are delivered.
C. Counting rule. 'Business day' for rescission purposes under §§ 1026.15 and 1026.23 means all calendar days except Sundays and legal public holidays (§ 1026.2(a)(6), second sentence — the rescission-specific definition, not the general 'offices open' definition). Count forward from the day after the last triggering event; the day of the event is day zero. Verify against the official interpretation's own example (Comment 23(a)(3)-1): consummation Friday, June 1, with disclosures and notice given Thursday, May 31 → Saturday = business day 1, Sunday excluded, Monday = 2, Tuesday = 3 → expires midnight Tuesday, June 5. Second example: disclosures and consummation Friday, June 1, notice given Monday, June 4 → Tuesday = 1, Wednesday = 2, Thursday = 3 → expires midnight Thursday, June 7.
D. Meaning of 'midnight.' Midnight at the END of the third business day — i.e., 12:00 a.m. entering the following calendar day. The right must be EXERCISED by then.
E. How to exercise. § 1026.23(a)(2): written notice by mail, telegram or other means of written communication; notice is given when MAILED, when filed for telegraphic transmission, or if sent by other means, when DELIVERED to the creditor's designated place of business. So a notice placed in the mail on the third business day is timely even if received later.
F. Added security interest edge case. Where a security interest in the principal dwelling is added to an existing obligation, the transaction is the ADDITION only; the creditor must deliver the § 1026.23(b) notice but need NOT deliver new material disclosures, and delivery of that notice alone begins the 3-business-day period (§ 1026.23(a)(1), last two sentences).

V. ANALYSIS — ASK 2 (EXTENDED WINDOW WHEN NOTICE OR MATERIAL DISCLOSURES ARE NEVER DELIVERED)
A. Trigger. 'If the required notice or material disclosures are not delivered' — i.e., either the § 1026.23(b) notice or one or more material disclosures is never delivered (or delivered so deficiently as not to be a delivery).
B. Three terminating events, earliest governs:
   1. 3 years after consummation (measured from consummation, not from discovery, not from the date the defect is cured);
   2. transfer of all of the consumer's interest in the property;
   3. sale of the property.
   The clause is 'whichever occurs first' — a cap, not an extension. Transfer or sale in year one terminates the right in year one.
C. The 3-year period is not a statute of limitations subject to equitable tolling. The Supreme Court so held as to 15 U.S.C. § 1635(f): Jesinoski v. Countrywide Home Loans, Inc., 575 U.S. 632 (2015). (Judicial gloss on the statute, not regulation text — flagged as such.)
D. Numeric illustration. Consummation Monday, March 3, 2025; no notice and no material disclosures ever delivered; no transfer or sale → right expires at midnight entering March 3, 2028 (the third-year anniversary of consummation), NOT three business days later and NOT extended by the 3-business-day rule.
E. Partial delivery. (i) Notice delivered but a material disclosure never delivered → the 3-business-day clock never starts, but the right still dies at the earliest of the three events in V.B. (ii) Both delivered, but late → ordinary window under Ask 1 runs 3 business days from the later delivery. (iii) Both delivered timely → ordinary window only; the 3-year backstop is inapplicable.
F. 'Material disclosures' for this purpose is a closed list, § 1026.23(a)(3)(ii): annual percentage rate, finance charge, amount financed, total of payments, payment schedule, and the disclosures and limitations referred to in §§ 1026.32(c) and (d) (high-cost mortgage) and 1026.43(g) (qualified mortgages). A defect outside that list does not open the extended window under this paragraph, however important it may be for other purposes.

VI. SIDE-BY-SIDE COMPARISON (consistency check)
                  | Ordinary window (§ 1026.23(a)(3)(i) sent. 1) | Extended window (sent. 2)
Start point       | last of the 3 triggering events             | consummation
Length            | 3 business days                              | 3 years (or earlier transfer/sale)
Selector          | WHICHEVER OCCURS LAST                        | WHICHEVER OCCURS FIRST
Terminal moment   | midnight at end of 3rd business day           | the earliest of the three events
The two figures (3 business days; 3 years) are both drawn from the same sentence and are alternatives, not additive. Do not describe the extended period as '3 years plus 3 business days.'

VII. WHAT THIS ANSWER DOES NOT COVER (flagged, not answered)
1. § 125(f) administrative-proceeding extension: the text says the period 'shall be extended in accordance with section 125(f) of the Act' but states no number; no number is stated here because none is in the cited provision.
2. Whether a non-judicial foreclosure, or a transfer subject to the mortgage, is a 'transfer of all of the consumer's interest in the property' — the regulation does not define the phrase.
3. Delivery presumptions and mailbox rules (when delivery is deemed complete) — a separate documentary question, not resolved by (a)(3)(i).
4. Consequences of rescission (voiding of the security interest, no liability for any amount including finance charge, 20-calendar-day return obligation) — § 1026.23(d), outside the two asks.
5. Whether state law or 15 U.S.C. § 1640 provides remedies running beyond the expiration of the right — a liability question, distinct from expiration.

VIII. ASSUMPTIONS
- Closed-end credit secured by the consumer's principal dwelling, not an exempt transaction under § 1026.23(f).
- The rule as codified is requested, not a litigated or judicially modified version (except where V.C expressly flags the Supreme Court's gloss).
- 'Material disclosures' carries the § 1026.23(a)(3)(ii) definition.
- No transaction-specific facts are supplied; the answer is the general rule.
- Text verified against four independent fetches of the current eCFR, the 2025 GovInfo CFR XML, and the CFPB's 2023-01-01 and 2020-12-28 versions; the (a)(3)(i) text is identical across them.
cautions: Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 23 on consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/2023-01-01/23 and 15 on consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/2020-12-28/15. The first reads: "See interpretation of 23(b)(1) Notice of Right To Rescind in Supplement I"

answer:
ANNUAL OCCUPATIONAL DOSE LIMITS FOR ADULT WORKERS — 10 CFR § 20.1201(a)

Governing text (current codified version; eCFR edition current through 12 Nov 2026; 2025 CFR vol. 1; source note 56 FR 23396, as amended through 72 FR 68059, Dec. 4, 2007):

  § 20.1201(a): "The licensee shall control the occupational dose to individual adults, except for planned special exposures under § 20.1206, to the following dose limits."

  (a)(1) An annual limit, which is the more limiting of—
     (i) The total effective dose equivalent being equal to 5 rems (0.05 Sv); or
     (ii) The sum of the deep-dose equivalent and the committed dose equivalent to any individual organ or tissue other than the lens of the eye being equal to 50 rems (0.5 Sv).

  (a)(2) The annual limits to the lens of the eye, to the skin of the whole body, and to the skin of the extremities, which are:
     (i) A lens dose equivalent of 15 rems (0.15 Sv), and
     (ii) A shallow-dose equivalent of 50 rem (0.5 Sv) to the skin of the whole body or to the skin of any extremity.

1. ANSWERS (the three requested limits)

  1.1 Total effective dose equivalent (TEDE) — § 20.1201(a)(1)(i)
      5 rems  =  0.05 Sv  (50 mSv)
      TEDE = effective dose equivalent from external sources + committed effective dose equivalent from intakes of radioactive material. It is the whole-body stochastic-risk limit.

  1.2 Lens of the eye — § 20.1201(a)(2)(i)
      15 rems  =  0.15 Sv  (150 mSv)
      Quantity is the lens dose equivalent, H_lens. It is a separate limit and is NOT included in the § 20.1201(a)(1) summation (see the NOTE to § 20.1202(a): "The dose equivalents for the lens of the eye, the skin, and the extremities are not included in the summation, but are subject to separate limits.").

  1.3 Skin of the whole body — § 20.1201(a)(2)(ii)
      50 rem  =  0.5 Sv  (500 mSv)
      Quantity is the shallow-dose equivalent, H_skin, averaged over the contiguous 10 square centimeters of skin receiving the highest exposure (§ 20.1201(c)). The same 50 rem (0.5 Sv) figure applies to the skin of any extremity; the extremity limit is not a separate, larger number under this paragraph.

2. UNIT CONVERSION BASIS
   The regulation prints both units in the codified text. The exact relationship used by the NRC is 1 Sv = 100 rem (1 rem = 0.01 Sv). Applying it:
      5 rem  x 0.01 = 0.05 Sv
      15 rem x 0.01 = 0.15 Sv
      50 rem x 0.01 = 0.50 Sv
   All three conversions agree with the parenthetical figures printed in the regulation itself; no rounding discrepancy exists. If millisieverts are wanted, multiply the Sv values by 1000: 50 mSv, 150 mSv, 500 mSv.

3. HOW THE THREE LIMITS INTERACT (needed so the 5 rem figure is not misapplied)
   - § 20.1201(a)(1) is a "more limiting of" test, not a sum: the licensee must satisfy whichever of (i) TEDE = 5 rem or (ii) deep-dose equivalent + committed dose equivalent to any organ/tissue other than the lens = 50 rems is more restrictive for the individual. The 5 rem TEDE value is not a universal absolute ceiling for every exposure pathway; the organ criterion can govern (e.g., a large deep-dose equivalent to a small portion of the body).
   - The lens (15 rems) and skin (50 rem) limits are additional, independent limits that must be met simultaneously and are excluded from the summation above.
   - Planned special exposures under § 20.1206 are excluded from the § 20.1201(a) control (see the opening words of (a)) and are governed by that section's separate constraints (not more than the numerical value of any § 20.1201(a) limit in any year, and not more than five times the annual limits over the individual's lifetime, § 20.1206(e)).
   - § 20.1201(f): the dose an individual may receive in the current year must be reduced by occupational dose received while employed by any other person.

4. VALUES IN THE SAME SUBSECTION THAT ARE COMMONLY CONFUSED WITH THE ABOVE
   - 50 rems (0.5 Sv) in (a)(1)(ii) is the deep-dose equivalent + committed dose equivalent to any individual organ or tissue other than the lens — a different quantity from the 50 rem (0.5 Sv) shallow-dose equivalent to skin in (a)(2)(ii), even though the numbers are identical.
   - Minors: 10 percent of the adult limits (§ 20.1207) — i.e., 0.5 rem TEDE, 1.5 rems lens, 5 rem skin.
   - Declared pregnant worker / embryo-fetus: 0.5 rem (0.005 Sv) over the gestation period (§ 20.1208) — separate from the adult occupational limits.
   - Members of the public: 0.1 rem (0.001 Sv) TEDE annual limit (§ 20.1301(a)(1)); not applicable to adult occupational exposure.
   - Monitoring thresholds (§ 20.1502(a)) are 10 percent of the § 20.1201(a) limits for adults, and are triggers for monitoring, not dose limits.

5. APPLICABILITY AND VERIFICATION CAVEATS
   - These are the NRC values as codified for NRC licensees. Agreement States adopt the same numerical limits in their regulations in virtually all cases, but the legally binding instrument for a specific site is the State's adopted rule and any license condition; verify against the governing jurisdiction's current rule text.
   - The lens value of 15 rems (0.15 Sv) is the value printed in the current codified text. International guidance (ICRP) recommends a lower lens limit equivalent to about 20 mSv per year averaged over defined periods; that recommendation is not the codified U.S. limit in § 20.1201(a) and is not substituted here. If a specific compliance year or a pending rulemaking matters, confirm against the eCFR edition in force for that year.
   - Citation to use: 10 CFR § 20.1201(a)(1)(i), (a)(2)(i), and (a)(2)(ii).

ANSWER — 29 CFR § 1926.501(b)(1), Unprotected Sides and Edges

1) TRIGGER HEIGHT
6 feet (1.8 m) or more above a lower level.

The duty attaches when the walking/working surface's unprotected side or edge is at or above 6 feet (1.8 m) above the lower level. The regulatory phrase is '6 feet (1.8 m) or more'; 6 feet exactly is within the trigger, not below it. Below 6 feet, § 1926.501(b)(1) does not require fall protection (other paragraphs of § 1926.501 and other subparts may still apply — see § 5 below).

2) REQUIRED SYSTEMS (the paragraph names three, in the alternative — any one satisfies it)
  (a) guardrail systems;
  (b) safety net systems; or
  (c) personal fall arrest systems.

3) CONTROLLING TEXT (verbatim, 29 CFR § 1926.501(b)(1), current eCFR / CFR 2025 Title 29 Vol. 8)

"(b) Protection from falling —
(1) Unprotected sides and edges. Each employee on a walking/working surface (horizontal and vertical surface) with an unprotected side or edge which is 6 feet (1.8 m) or more above a lower level shall be protected from falling by the use of guardrail systems, safety net systems, or personal fall arrest systems."

4) SCOPE OF THE PARAGRAPH AS WRITTEN
- Applies to 'each employee on a walking/working surface (horizontal and vertical surface)' — the parenthetical is part of the regulation and is not limited to floors or roofs.
- Applies to an 'unprotected side or edge' — i.e., an edge without an existing guardrail, wall, or equivalent barrier. If a compliant guardrail system already exists at the edge, the edge is not unprotected and (b)(1) is satisfied by that system.
- The three systems are alternatives; the employer may select any one (or a combination). The paragraph does not rank them.
- Design/performance criteria for each named system are in § 1926.502: guardrail systems § 1926.502(b); safety net systems § 1926.502(c); personal fall arrest systems § 1926.502(d). A system that is installed but does not meet § 1926.502 criteria does not satisfy (b)(1).
- Training in the systems is required by § 1926.503.
- Note that the (b)(1) text itself contains no exception and no fall protection plan alternative; the infeasibility/greater-hazard exception and § 1926.502(k) fall protection plan alternative appear in (b)(2)(i) (leading edges) and in other specific paragraphs, not in (b)(1).

5) BOUNDARY WITH ADJACENT PROVISIONS (so the 6 ft / three-system answer is not misapplied)
§ 1926.501(b)(1) governs the general case of an unprotected side or edge. Other paragraphs of the same section name different system sets for specific operations, and those paragraphs control where they apply:
- (b)(2) leading edges — same 6 ft trigger, same three systems, plus the infeasibility/greater-hazard exception and § 1926.502(k) plan.
- (b)(4) holes (including skylights) — personal fall arrest systems, covers, or guardrails around the hole.
- (b)(5) formwork and reinforcing steel — personal fall arrest systems, safety net systems, or positioning device systems.
- (b)(6) ramps, runways, other walkways — guardrail systems.
- (b)(7)(ii) wells, pits, shafts, similar excavations — guardrail systems, fences, barricades, or covers.
- (b)(8) dangerous equipment — guardrails/equipment guards below 6 ft; guardrails, personal fall arrest, or safety nets at 6 ft or more.
- (b)(9) overhand bricklaying — the three systems or a controlled access zone.
- (b)(14) wall openings — guardrail, safety net, or personal fall arrest, on the stated 6 ft outer / 39 in. (1.0 m) inner geometry.
- (b)(15) walking/working surfaces not otherwise addressed — guardrail, safety net, or personal fall arrest at 6 ft (1.8 m) or more.
Where none of (b)(1)–(b)(14) fits, (b)(15) supplies the same 6 ft trigger and the same three systems as (b)(1).

6) SOURCE AND REVISION CONTROL
The quoted text was taken from the current eCFR rendering of 29 CFR § 1926.501 and cross-checked against the GovInfo CFR 2025 edition (Title 29, Vol. 8, § 1926.501), both retrieved 2026-11-17. The answer above is tied to that revision. If this answer is to be cited in a compliance document, re-verify against the then-current eCFR text, because Part 1926 is amended periodically.

7) ONE-LINE RESTATEMENT FOR USE IN A DOCUMENT OR TRAINING SLIDE
Under 29 CFR § 1926.501(b)(1), each employee on a walking/working surface with an unprotected side or edge 6 feet (1.8 m) or more above a lower level must be protected from falling by guardrail systems, safety net systems, or personal fall arrest systems.

question: P10
answer:
LEGAL NOTE — Working Time Regulations 1998 (SI 1998/1833), reg 4(1): maximum weekly working time and the individual opt-out

Scope: England and Wales and Scotland (the provision is marked E+W+S); adult workers; the rule as it stands in the revised text, i.e. as amended by SI 1999/3372, SI 2002/3128 and SI 2023/1426. Not the separate young-worker limits in reg 4(2)-adjacent provisions, and not a compliance determination on any individual's facts.

1. THE LIMIT (ask 1)

Reg 4(1), as substituted by SI 1999/3372 reg 3(1)(a), reads:

  'Unless his employer has first obtained the worker's agreement in writing to perform such work, a worker's working time, including overtime, in any reference period which is applicable in his case shall not exceed an average of 48 hours for each seven days.'

Therefore the headline limit is 48 hours per seven days, averaged across the reference period, with overtime expressly inside the calculation. Four points of construction:

(a) It is an average, not a weekly cap. A worker may lawfully work more than 48 hours in any given week provided the average across the reference period does not exceed 48. The Regulations create no free-standing offence of working a long week.
(b) 'Working time' takes its reg 2 meaning (time working, at the employer's disposal and carrying out activities or duties; plus time on relevant training and certain travel); 'including overtime' makes clear that hours beyond contractual normal hours count.
(c) The reference period (reg 4(3)-(5)):
    - default: any period of 17 weeks in the course of employment (reg 4(3)(b));
    - where a relevant agreement provides for application to successive periods of 17 weeks: each such period (reg 4(3)(a));
    - subject to any agreement under reg 23(b) (see paragraph 5 below);
    - worker employed for less than 17 weeks: the period since starting work (reg 4(4));
    - worker excluded from certain provisions by reg 21 (transport/sea-fishing/offshore-type sectors): 17 weeks is read as 26 weeks (reg 4(5)).
(d) Arithmetic ceilings that follow directly from 48 hours per seven days:
    - 17-week reference period: 48 × 17 = 816 hours
    - 26-week reference period (reg 21 workers): 48 × 26 = 1,248 hours
    - 52 weeks, if a reg 23(b) agreement so provides: 48 × 52 = 2,496 hours

Calculation formula (reg 4(6)): average = (A + B) / C, where A = aggregate hours of working time during the reference period; B = aggregate hours in the period immediately after the reference period ending when the number of days worked in that subsequent period equals the number of 'excluded days' in the reference period; C = number of weeks in the reference period.

'Excluded days' (reg 4(7)): days in (a) annual leave under reg 13, 13A or 15B; (b) sick leave; (c) maternity, paternity, adoption or parental leave; and (d) any period in respect of which the reg 4(1) limit did not apply because the employer had obtained the worker's written agreement. The B component and the excluded-days definition are what stop leave and opted-out weeks from diluting the average.

Worked checks (both consistent with the 816-hour ceiling):
  - Within the limit: 10 weeks at 50 hours plus 7 weeks at 40 hours = 500 + 280 = 780 hours; 780 / 17 = 45.88 hours per seven days — compliant, despite ten weeks above 48.
  - Outside the limit: 17 weeks totalling 830 hours; 830 / 17 = 48.82 hours per seven days — breach of reg 4(1) absent an agreement.

Employer's duty (reg 4(2)): the employer must take all reasonable steps, in keeping with the need to protect health and safety, to secure compliance for each worker to whom the limit applies, and must keep up-to-date records of all workers who carry out work to which the limit does not apply because a reg 4(1) agreement has been obtained.

2. HOW A WORKER IS TAKEN OUTSIDE THE LIMIT (ask 2)

The single mechanism in reg 4(1) itself is the individual opt-out: the limit does not apply where 'the employer has first obtained the worker's agreement in writing to perform such work'. Reg 5 ('Agreement to exclude the maximum') supplies the terms:

  Reg 5(2): an agreement for the purposes of reg 4 — (a) may either relate to a specified period or apply indefinitely; and (b) subject to any provision in the agreement for a different period of notice, shall be terminable by the worker by giving not less than seven days' notice to his employer in writing.
  Reg 5(3): where the agreement provides for termination after a period of notice, that notice period shall not exceed three months.
  Reg 5(1) and 5(4) were omitted by SI 1999/3372 and are spent.

Practical steps, in order:
  1. The employer must obtain the agreement before the worker performs the work in question ('first obtained ... to perform such work'). A purported ratification after the event does not satisfy reg 4(1).
  2. The agreement must be in writing and must be the individual worker's own agreement — it is not a collective or workforce agreement, and it is not implied from a contract term that merely permits overtime.
  3. The agreement should state whether it is for a specified period or indefinite, and any notice period for termination; if a notice period is specified it must not exceed three months (reg 5(3)); if none is specified, the worker may terminate on seven days' written notice (reg 5(2)(b)).
  4. The employer must record the worker in its up-to-date records of opted-out workers (reg 4(2), as amended).
  5. The worker may withdraw: on seven days' written notice, or such longer period as the agreement specifies, capped at three months. Once the agreement is terminated, reg 4(1) applies again from the effective date; the worker cannot be kept outside the limit thereafter on the strength of the terminated agreement.

Effect and limits of the opt-out:
  - It disapplies reg 4(1) only. It does not disapply the reg 6 eight-hour average for night workers, the reg 10 rest-break entitlements, the reg 11 weekly rest period, the reg 12 in-work rest break or the 4 weeks' (5.6 weeks as amended) annual leave entitlement. Days covered by an opt-out are 'excluded days' for reg 4(6)-(7) purposes.
  - It is personal to the worker and revocable; a refusal to sign, or a withdrawal, does not entitle the employer to treat the worker less favourably. (The detriment protection is in regs 31-32; that citation is NOT drawn from the fetched passages and should be checked before it is relied on in a live matter.)
  - Exceeding 48 hours on an opt-out does not create a contractual entitlement to that work; the contract, and the employer's health-and-safety duties under the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974, continue to apply.

3. WHAT THIS IS NOT
  - Not a sectoral or collective exemption. Reg 5 as amended deals only with the individual agreement; the only other route by which the reference period (not the 48-hour average) can be altered is a relevant agreement under reg 23(b), which reg 4(3) expressly contemplates. The commonly stated effect of reg 23(b) — permitting a reference period longer than 17 weeks, up to 52 weeks — is consistent with reg 4(3) but the 52-week figure itself is not in the fetched text and should be verified against reg 23 before being quoted.
  - Not a defence to the other working-time limits. Reg 6 (8 hours per 24 for night workers) is a separate limit with its own reference period and is not subject to reg 5.
  - Not enforced by a stand-alone 'excess hours' offence; the Regulations are health-and-safety legislation enforced by HSE/local authorities, and the individual remedies lie mainly in the rest-break/leave provisions and in the detriment provisions. (Enforcement route: not drawn from the fetched passages; verify regs 28-32.)

4. VERIFICATION TABLE
  - '48 hours for each seven days, including overtime' — reg 4(1), fetched text. VERIFIED.
  - 'Averaged over the reference period' — reg 4(1) and 4(6), fetched text. VERIFIED.
  - '17 weeks default; period since start if employed <17 weeks; 26 weeks for reg 21 workers' — reg 4(3)-(5), fetched text. VERIFIED.
  - 'Excluded days: annual leave, sick leave, maternity/paternity/adoption/parental leave, opted-out periods' — reg 4(7), fetched text. VERIFIED.
  - 'Formula (A+B)/C' — reg 4(6), fetched text. VERIFIED.
  - 'Employer records duty for opted-out workers' — reg 4(2) as amended, fetched text. VERIFIED.
  - 'Written individual agreement, obtained first; specified period or indefinite; seven days' written notice to terminate; notice period capped at three months' — reg 4(1) and reg 5(2)-(3), fetched text. VERIFIED.
  - 'Reg 23(b) longer reference period (up to 52 weeks)', 'regs 31-32 detriment protection', 'HSE/local authority enforcement' — NOT in the fetched passages; stated as recollection and flagged for verification.

5. ONE-LINE ANSWERS
  (1) 48 hours per seven days, averaged over the applicable reference period, with overtime included (reg 4(1)).
  (2) By the employer first obtaining the worker's own written agreement to perform such work — the individual opt-out under reg 4(1), with its terms governed by reg 5(2)-(3): specified period or indefinite, terminable by the worker on not less than seven days' written notice unless the agreement provides otherwise, and in any event with a notice period not exceeding three months.

question: P12
answer:
RECORD RETENTION UNDER 21 CFR 211.180(a) — CONTROLLING TEXT AND ANSWER

1. CONTROLLING REGULATORY TEXT (verbatim, 21 CFR 211.180(a))

"(a) Any production, control, or distribution record that is required to be maintained in compliance with this part and is specifically associated with a batch of a drug product shall be retained for at least 1 year after the expiration date of the batch or, in the case of certain OTC drug products lacking expiration dating because they meet the criteria for exemption under Sec. 211.137, 3 years after distribution of the batch."

Source citation line for the section: [43 FR 45077, Sept. 29, 1978, as amended at 60 FR 4091, Jan. 20, 1995]. Text verified as identical across three renderings: eCFR current (title 21, chapter I, subchapter C, part 211, subpart J, Sec. 211.180), GovInfo CFR-2025-title21-vol4 print (Sec. 211.180), and the GovInfo XML for the same section. No amendment to Sec. 211.180(a) is pending in the retrieved material.

2. ANSWERS

Ask 1 — Batch-specific production, control, or distribution records (drug products with expiration dating):
RETAIN FOR AT LEAST 1 YEAR AFTER THE EXPIRATION DATE OF THE BATCH.
- Value: 1. Unit: year. Trigger event: the expiration date of that batch.
- "At least" is operative: 1 year is a federal floor, not a target. Longer retention may be compelled by other sources (see Section 6).

Ask 2 — Certain OTC drug products lacking expiration dating:
RETAIN FOR AT LEAST 3 YEARS AFTER DISTRIBUTION OF THE BATCH.
- Value: 3. Unit: years. Trigger event: distribution of the batch (not manufacture, not release, not shipment receipt by the customer).
- The 3-year clock applies only to OTC drug products that lack expiration dating *because they meet the criteria for exemption under Sec. 211.137*. An OTC product that has an expiration date is governed by the 1-year-after-expiration-date rule in the first branch of (a), not by the 3-year branch. A product that lacks an expiration date for some reason other than the Sec. 211.137 exemption is not covered by the second branch as written and should be treated as a compliance gap to resolve (see Section 5).

3. DECISION TABLE — WHICH CLOCK APPLIES

| Product situation | Clock start | Minimum retention |
|---|---|---|
| Rx or OTC drug product with an expiration date; batch-specific production, control, or distribution record | Expiration date of the batch | 1 year after that date |
| OTC drug product exempt from expiration dating under Sec. 211.137; batch-specific production, control, or distribution record | Date the batch is distributed | 3 years after that date |
| Components, drug product containers, closures, labeling (not batch-specific; governed by 211.180(b)) | Expiration date, or for Sec. 211.137-exempt OTC, distribution of the LAST lot using the item | 1 year after expiration date, or 3 years after distribution of the last lot |
| Complaint files (governed by 211.198(b), not 211.180(a)) | Expiration date or date complaint received, whichever is later; for Sec. 211.137-exempt OTC, distribution | 1 year after the later of the two; 3 years after distribution for exempt OTC |
| Reserve samples (governed by 211.170, not 211.180(a)) | Expiration date; distribution for exempt OTC | 1 year after expiration date; 3 months/6 months for radioactive; 3 years after distribution for exempt OTC |

4. SCOPE QUALIFIERS THAT MUST ACCOMPANY THE ANSWER

(a) 'Specifically associated with a batch.' The 1-year/3-year rule in 211.180(a) attaches to records tied to an identified batch. Records not so tied are governed elsewhere in part 211 (e.g., master production and control records under 211.186, which carry no stated retention period in 211.180(a); component/container/closure/labeling records under 211.180(b)). Do not apply the (a) periods by analogy without checking the governing section.

(b) 'Required to be maintained in compliance with this part.' The retention duty runs to CGMP-required records (e.g., batch production and control records under 211.188, laboratory records under 211.194, distribution records under 211.196), not to every business document a firm happens to hold.

(c) Form of record and accessibility. Per 211.180(c), records or copies must be readily available for authorized inspection during the retention period at the establishment where the recorded activities occurred, and are subject to photocopying/reproduction; records immediately retrievable by computer or other electronic means from another location satisfy (c). Per 211.180(d), original records or true copies (photocopies, microfilm, microfiche, or other accurate reproductions) are acceptable, with reader/photocopy equipment readily available where reduction techniques are used.

(d) Minimum, not maximum. Nothing in 211.180(a) authorizes destruction at the stated period if another obligation requires longer retention.

5. APPLICATION NOTES / WORKED EXAMPLES

- Expiring batch: expiration date 31 March 2027 -> retain the batch-specific production, control, and distribution records until at least 31 March 2028.
- Sec. 211.137-exempt OTC batch: distributed 15 June 2026 -> retain until at least 15 June 2029.
- Partial distribution: where a batch is distributed in more than one shipment, the conservative and inspection-defensible reading is to run the 3 years from the last distribution of that batch, so no portion of the batch's record set is destroyed while any of the batch remains within its retention window. Document the date chosen and the basis in the retention procedure.
- Product whose expiration-dating exemption is later withdrawn or who adds expiration dating: the clock reverts to the expiration-date branch for batches that carry an expiration date. Do not blend the two clocks for a single batch.
- Missing Sec. 211.137 basis: if a product lacks expiration dating without a documented Sec. 211.137 exemption basis, the 3-year branch does not apply by its terms. Treat as a deviation to be corrected (establish the exemption basis or assign expiration dating) rather than as license to use 3 years.

6. WHAT THIS ANSWER DOES NOT COVER (outside 211.180(a))

The regulation sets a federal minimum. Longer retention can be required or prudent because of: applicable statutes of limitation; state licensing or recordkeeping law; contractual or customer quality agreements; marketing authorization or ANDA/NDA commitments; 21 CFR Part 11 audit-trail and electronic-record obligations; litigation holds; and, for biological products, 21 CFR 600.12(b), which sets different periods. Non-U.S. GDP/GMP requirements (e.g., EU Annex 11 / Chapter 4, or local 1-year-after-expiry-plus rules) may also exceed these periods. None of these alters the two values above; each must be checked separately and the firm's retention schedule set at the longest applicable period.

7. COMPLIANCE-READY STATEMENT (suitable for an SOP or inspection response)

"Batch-specific production, control, and distribution records required by 21 CFR Part 211 are retained for at least 1 year after the expiration date of the batch, in accordance with 21 CFR 211.180(a). For OTC drug products that lack expiration dating because they meet the criteria for exemption under 21 CFR 211.137, such records are retained for at least 3 years after distribution of the batch. Records are maintained in a form and at a location that satisfies 21 CFR 211.180(c) and (d) and are retained longer where another applicable requirement so demands."
