# 40 CFR § 50.19 — 8-hour primary ozone NAAQS: level and site-level test

## 1. The level (ask 1)

**0.070 ppm, daily maximum 8-hour average.**

Verbatim, § 50.19(a) (current eCFR text, identical in govinfo 2024/2025 CFR and Cornell LII):

> "(a) The level of the national 8-hour primary ambient air quality standard for ozone (O3) is 0.070 parts per million (ppm), daily maximum 8-hour average, measured by a reference method based on appendix D to this part and designated in accordance with part 53 of this chapter or an equivalent method designated in accordance with part 53 of this chapter."

Three components are inseparable in the regulatory text and must be carried together in any citation of the level:

| Component | Value |
|---|---|
| Indicator / averaging time | O3, daily maximum 8-hour average |
| Level | 0.070 ppm (equivalently 70 ppb) |
| Measurement method | Reference method based on 40 CFR part 50, appendix D, designated under part 53; **or** an equivalent method (FEM) designated under part 53 |

Unit note: the regulation states the level in **ppm**. 0.070 ppm = 70 ppb exactly. For context only (not a regulatory figure), 0.070 ppm ≈ 137 µg/m³ using 1 ppm O3 ≈ 1,960 µg/m³ at 25 °C and 1 atm. All compliance comparisons should be made in ppm/ppb, not in the converted mass concentration.

## 2. When the standard is met at a monitoring site (ask 2)

**Met when the 3-year average of the annual fourth-highest daily maximum 8-hour average O3 concentration is less than or equal to 0.070 ppm, as determined in accordance with appendix U to part 50.**

Verbatim, § 50.19(b):

> "(b) The 8-hour primary O3 ambient air quality standard is met at an ambient air quality monitoring site when the 3-year average of the annual fourth-highest daily maximum 8-hour average O3 concentration is less than or equal to 0.070 ppm, as determined in accordance with appendix U to this part."

Structural points that the sentence encodes:

1. **It is a site-level test**, applied monitor by monitor — not an area-wide attainment determination. Area attainment/unclassifiable designations are made under Clean Air Act § 107 and codified at 40 CFR part 81, drawing on monitor design values plus other factors; that is a separate question from whether the standard "is met at a monitoring site."
2. **The compared quantity is a 3-year average**, not a single year and not a single day. The annual metric that enters the average is the **fourth-highest** daily maximum 8-hour average of that year — i.e., a single year may record up to three days above 0.070 ppm and still contribute a fourth-high value at or below 0.070 ppm.
3. **The comparison is `≤ 0.070 ppm`** — a design value exactly equal to 0.070 ppm meets the standard.
4. **"As determined in accordance with appendix U"** makes Appendix U (Interpretation of the Primary and Secondary National Ambient Air Quality Standards for Ozone) part of the test: Appendix U supplies the data-handling, completeness, and rounding conventions. Appendix P also remains in the CFR, but it interprets the *earlier* ozone standards; for the current (2015) 8-hour standard, Appendix U is the operative interpretive appendix.

## 3. Version / effective date — state this alongside the number

The current text carries the source note **[80 FR 65452, Oct. 26, 2015]**, i.e., the 2015 ozone NAAQS review, which set the 8-hour primary standard at 0.070 ppm. § 50.19 has been amended more than once, and the level differs across versions; if the determination must be made as of a historical date (e.g., a State Implementation Plan obligation, a nonattainment designation, or an anti-backsliding analysis), the applicable level is the one in § 50.19 **as it read on that date**, not the current 0.070 ppm. Background (general knowledge, *not* from the retrieved passages — verify against the Federal Register before relying on it): the 2008 revision set 0.075 ppm and the 1997 revision set 0.08 ppm.

## 4. Procedure for making the site-level call

1. **Hourly data → daily maximum 8-hour average.** Compute 8-hour running averages from valid hourly O3 concentrations per the appendix D reference-method data conventions; the daily maximum 8-hour average is the highest valid 8-hour average for that calendar day.
2. **Assemble the annual series.** For each year, compile the daily maximum 8-hour averages across the site's ozone monitoring season (season and monitoring obligations come from 40 CFR part 58, not from § 50.19).
3. **Apply data completeness.** Appendix U governs whether a year's data are complete enough to yield a valid annual fourth-high. (Appendix U's specific completeness percentage and incomplete-year rules are not reproduced in the retrieved passages — read them from the appendix text; do not infer them from § 50.19.)
4. **Take the annual fourth-highest** daily maximum 8-hour average for each of three consecutive years.
5. **Average the three annual fourth-high values** to obtain the design value.
6. **Round, then compare.** Appendix U specifies the rounding convention for the design value (EPA practice under the 2015 standard is to round the 3-year average to three decimal places, i.e., nearest 0.001 ppm, before comparison — confirm the exact wording in Appendix U). Compare the rounded value to 0.070 ppm: **≤ 0.070 ppm → standard met; > 0.070 ppm → standard not met** (a violation).
7. **Data treatment.** Air quality data influenced by exceptional events may be excluded only in accordance with 40 CFR § 50.14 (EPA concurrence or, where applicable, the regulatory exclusion process); excluded data do not enter steps 1–5. Wildfire and stratospheric ozone intrusion events are the common ozone cases.

## 5. Secondary standard (for completeness — same section)

§ 50.19(c) sets the national **secondary** 8-hour O3 standard at the same 0.070 ppm, daily maximum 8-hour average, with the same measurement-method requirement, and § 50.19(d) applies the identical site-level test (3-year average of the annual fourth-highest daily maximum 8-hour average ≤ 0.070 ppm, per Appendix U). Primary and secondary are numerically identical for ozone, but they are separate standards and should be cited separately.

## 6. One-paragraph answer as it would appear in a regulatory document

Under 40 CFR § 50.19(a), the level of the national 8-hour primary ambient air quality standard for ozone is 0.070 ppm, daily maximum 8-hour average, measured by an appendix D reference method designated under part 53 or an equivalent method designated under part 53. Under § 50.19(b), that standard is met at an ambient air quality monitoring site when the 3-year average of the annual fourth-highest daily maximum 8-hour average O3 concentration is less than or equal to 0.070 ppm, as determined in accordance with 40 CFR part 50, appendix U. (Secondary standard: § 50.19(c)–(d), same level and same form.)

## 7. Points a reviewer should verify before external use

- Appendix U's exact completeness and rounding language — cited here as the controlling reference but not quoted, because it was not among the retrieved passages.
- The effective date of the 2015 revision (the rule text gives the *Federal Register* citation, 80 FR 65452, Oct. 26, 2015, but not the effective date) if a date-specific obligation turns on it.
- Whether the intended question is the site-level test (answered here) or an area designation under CAA § 107 / 40 CFR part 81 (not answered here).

LEGAL ANSWER — 29 C.F.R. § 825.200(a)

1. Amount of FMLA leave. Under § 825.200(a), an eligible employee's FMLA leave entitlement—except in the case of leave to care for a covered servicemember with a serious injury or illness—is limited to a total of 12 workweeks of leave during any 12-month period. The 12 workweeks are a single aggregate cap for any one or more of the five qualifying reasons listed in § 825.200(a)(1)–(5): birth of the employee's son or daughter and care for the newborn; placement of a son or daughter for adoption or foster care and care for the newly placed child; care for the employee's spouse, son, daughter, or parent with a serious health condition; the employee's own serious health condition making the employee unable to perform one or more essential functions of the job; and a qualifying exigency arising from a family member's covered active duty or call to covered active duty. The entitlement is not 12 workweeks per reason; it is 12 workweeks total for any one or more of those reasons during the applicable 12-month period.

2. Period over which the entitlement is measured. Section 825.200(a) states the period as 'any 12-month period.' Section 825.200(b) permits the employer to choose the method for determining that 12-month period from four options: (1) the calendar year; (2) any fixed 12-month leave year, such as a fiscal year, a year required by state law, or a year starting on the employee's anniversary date; (3) the 12-month period measured forward from the date any employee's first FMLA leave under paragraph (a) begins; or (4) a 'rolling' 12-month period measured backward from the date an employee uses any FMLA leave as described in paragraph (a). The regulation does not itself require a rolling period; the employer selects one of these methods and applies it. Accordingly, the correct general statement is 12 workweeks during any 12-month period, with the 12-month period determined by the employer's selected method under § 825.200(b).

3. Effect of the exclusion for leave to care for a covered servicemember. The question directs that leave to care for a covered servicemember be left aside. That is the military caregiver leave entitlement under § 825.200(f): 26 workweeks of leave during a single 12-month period to care for a covered servicemember with a serious injury or illness, measured forward from the date the employee's first such leave begins. Section 825.200(a) expressly excepts that leave from the 12-workweek limit. The combined 26-workweek limit in § 825.200(g) during that single 12-month period is likewise outside the scope of this answer.

4. Qualifications. This is the regulatory entitlement ceiling, not a determination of employee eligibility under the FMLA's eligibility provisions or of an employee's remaining leave balance. Actual available leave is reduced by FMLA leave already used during the applicable 12-month period. The answer assumes no more generous state-law or employer-policy entitlement and does not address the special airline flight crew calculation in § 825.802.

Conclusion: 12 workweeks of FMLA leave during any 12-month period, with the 12-month period determined by the employer under § 825.200(b), leaving aside the separate 26-workweek military caregiver entitlement under § 825.200(f).

answer:
SMTP LINE-LENGTH LIMITS UNDER RFC 5321 SECTION 4.5.3.1

=== 1. HEADLINE ANSWER ===

| Object | RFC 5321 section | Max total length | What the count includes | What it does not include |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| SMTP text line (a line of message content sent in DATA) | 4.5.3.1.6 | 1000 octets | every octet of the line's text as transmitted, plus the terminating <CRLF> (2 octets) | the extra leading dot duplicated for transparency (dot-stuffing) |
| Reply line | 4.5.3.1.5 | 512 octets | the 3-digit reply code, the separator ("-" on a continuation line, <SP> on the final line), the reply text, plus the terminating <CRLF> | nothing relevant; the code and separator are inside the 512 |
| Command line (for contrast) | 4.5.3.1.4 | 512 octets | the command word (e.g. MAIL), the <SP>, all parameters/arguments, plus the terminating <CRLF> | nothing relevant |

Answer to ask 1: an SMTP text line is limited to 1000 octets total, inclusive of <CRLF>.
If the questioner instead means the command/transaction line, that is 512 octets inclusive of <CRLF>; the two figures are different objects and must not be interchanged.

=== 2. VERBATIM NORMATIVE TEXT (RFC 5321, October 2008) ===

4.5.3.1.4.  Command Line
"The maximum total length of a command line including the command word and the <CRLF> is 512 octets.  SMTP extensions may be used to increase this limit."

4.5.3.1.5.  Reply Line
"The maximum total length of a reply line including the reply code and the <CRLF> is 512 octets.  More information may be conveyed through multiple-line replies."

4.5.3.1.6.  Text Line
"The maximum total length of a text line including the <CRLF> is 1000 octets (not counting the leading dot duplicated for transparency).  This number may be increased by the use of SMTP Service Extensions."

Adjacent items in the same section, for context only: local-part 64 octets (4.5.3.1.1), domain 255 octets (4.5.3.1.2), path 256 octets including punctuation and separators (4.5.3.1.3), message content at least 64K octets (4.5.3.1.7).

=== 3. WHAT THE COUNTS INCLUDE (ask 2, in detail) ===

3.1 Common to all three: the terminating <CRLF> is inside the number.
The <CRLF> is 2 octets (CR = 0x0D, LF = 0x0A). Every one of the three sentences says "including ... the <CRLF>". Therefore the usable payload is always 2 octets less than the headline figure. Any tool that appends CRLF after filling a 1000- or 512-octet buffer is off by two and will emit non-conforming lines.

3.2 Text line (4.5.3.1.6) - 1000 octets includes:
  - the entire content of that line as it appears on the wire after transparency processing is undone at the receiver, i.e. the message text octets themselves (header lines and body lines alike - the 1000-octet limit applies to every line of the message content, including each header line);
  - the terminating <CRLF>.
Text line - explicitly excluded:
  - "the leading dot duplicated for transparency": when a content line begins with ".", the sender prepends one extra "." (dot-stuffing) and the receiver removes it. That added dot is NOT counted against the 1000. So a conforming line may occupy 1001 octets on the wire (998 counted content octets + 1 transparency dot + CRLF).
  - The end-of-data indicator (a line consisting of a single "." followed by CRLF) is not a text line at all and is not counted against this limit.
  - It is not a per-message limit: it applies per line, independently, to every line.

3.3 Reply line (4.5.3.1.5) - 512 octets includes:
  - the reply code: exactly 3 digits (RFC 5321 ABNF: Reply-code = %x32-35 %x30-35 %x30-39, i.e. 200-599);
  - the separator character: "-" (hyphen/minus) when the line is a non-final line of a multiline reply, or <SP> on the final line (clients must also tolerate a bare code with no <SP>);
  - the reply text (RFC 5321 ABNF: textstring = 1*(%d09 / %d32-126), i.e. HT, SP and printable US-ASCII only);
  - the terminating <CRLF>.
Reply line - scope notes:
  - The 512 limit is per line, not per reply. A multiline reply may be arbitrarily long in total; each of its lines independently must be <= 512 octets. "More information may be conveyed through multiple-line replies" is the RFC's own instruction for exceeding the text budget.
  - The space following the reply code is part of the text, not extra (RFC 5321 4.2: "The space (blank) following the reply code is considered part of the text").

3.4 Command line (4.5.3.1.4) - 512 octets includes:
  - the command word (HELO, EHLO, MAIL, RCPT, DATA, RSET, VRFY, EXPN, HELP, NOOP, QUIT, or an extension verb);
  - the separating <SP>;
  - all parameters, including the angle brackets of a path and any ESMTP parameters;
  - the terminating <CRLF>.

=== 4. DERIVED PAYLOAD BUDGETS (arithmetic check) ===

| Line type | Total limit | minus CRLF | Max payload before CRLF |
|---|---|---|---|
| Text line | 1000 | -2 | 998 octets of content (plus 1 uncounted dot if the line starts with '.') |
| Command line | 512 | -2 | 510 octets of command text (verb + SP + parameters) |
| Reply line | 512 | -2 | 509 octets of code+separator+text; with a separator present: 3 + 1 + 506 |

Checks: 998 + 2 = 1000. 510 + 2 = 512. 3 + 1 + 506 + 2 = 512. A bare reply code ("250" + CRLF) is 5 octets.

=== 5. WORKED WIRE EXAMPLES ===

E1 (text line, at the limit): 998 content octets not starting with '.' -> 998 + CRLF = 1000 octets on the wire. Conforming, exactly at the limit.
E2 (text line, over): 999 content octets + CRLF = 1001 octets, line does not start with '.' -> non-conforming; the sender must wrap or shorten it.
E3 (text line, dot-stuffed, still conforming): 998 content octets whose first octet is '.' -> transmitted as '.' + '.' + 996 further octets = 999 octets, + CRLF = 1001 octets on the wire. Conforming: the duplicated dot is excluded by 4.5.3.1.6.
E4 (reply line, at the limit): "250-" + 506 octets of text + CRLF = 3 + 1 + 506 + 2 = 512. Conforming. Same line as a final line uses <SP> instead of "-" and is again 512.
E5 (command line, at the limit): 510 octets of "MAIL FROM:<...>" text + CRLF = 512. Conforming.

=== 6. IMPLEMENTATION SIZING (follows directly from the above) ===

- Command/reply read buffer: hold 512 octets per line; use 513 so that a line arriving without CRLF within 512 octets is detectable and can be answered with a 500-class reply rather than silently accepted.
- DATA line read buffer: the worst conforming wire line is 1001 octets (E3). Use 1002: it holds every conforming line and leaves one octet of headroom to detect an over-long line before the CRLF.
- Do not use a single 512-octet buffer for DATA: it truncates legal 1000-octet text lines. Do not use 1000 for the command channel: it silently accepts non-conforming long commands.

=== 7. OCTETS, NOT CHARACTERS ===

The RFC consistently says "octets". With 8-bit or internationalized content (8BITMIME, SMTPUTF8), a 998-octet line may be far fewer than 998 characters. The current revision text states the point explicitly: "lengths, rather than character counts, are intended." Do not size buffers or validate in characters.

=== 8. CONFORMANCE SEMANTICS (paraphrase - not a verbatim quote) ===

RFC 5321 4.5.3.1 frames these figures as minimum maximums: an implementation MUST be able to receive objects at least this large, and must not send objects larger than this unless an extension has raised the limit. They are therefore floors on receiver capability and ceilings on sender output, not mere recommendations. 4.5.3.1.4 and 4.5.3.1.6 both state that SMTP extensions may increase the figure (e.g. a SIZE/line-length extension); absent negotiation, the base figures bind. The 500 reply code's example list in 4.2.2 includes "command line too long", which is the intended response to an over-long command.

=== 9. VERSION / REVISION STATUS ===

The figures are stable. RFC 5321 (October 2008, which obsoletes RFC 2821) gives 512 / 512 / 1000. The in-progress revision (draft-ietf-emailcore-rfc5321bis-44) carries the identical text for 4.5.3.1.4, 4.5.3.1.5 and 4.5.3.1.6, so no revision of the source changes the answer. Cite section 4.5.3.1.6 for the text line, 4.5.3.1.5 for the reply line, 4.5.3.1.4 for the command line, so the reader can verify each figure independently.

=== 10. COMMON PITFALLS THIS ANSWER GUARDS AGAINST ===

1. Quoting 512 as "the SMTP line length" without qualification - that is the command/reply line, not the DATA text line.
2. Quoting 1000 for command lines, which then accepts non-conforming input.
3. Forgetting the CRLF is inside the number (off-by-two in every buffer).
4. Counting the dot-stuffing dot and rejecting legal lines (E3).
5. Applying 512 to the whole of a multiline reply instead of to each of its lines.
6. Counting characters instead of octets under 8BITMIME/SMTPUTF8.
7. Treating the figures as recommendations rather than as mandatory minimum-maximums.
